content: COTL1, also known as coactosin-like protein (CLP), is a protein in humans encoded by the COTL1 gene. This protein is one of the many actin-binding proteins that play a role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. It specifically binds to filamentous actin (F-actin) and interacts with 5-lipoxygenase (ALOX5), stabilizing this enzyme. Although the COTL1 gene has been reported to map to chromosome 17 in the Smith-Magenis syndrome region, the most accurate alignments place it on chromosome 16. The Smith-Magenis syndrome region contains two related pseudogenes. COTL1 has been demonstrated to interact with ALOX5, which is the first committed enzyme in the metabolic pathway of arachidonic acid. This pathway produces several biologically significant cell signaling molecules, including: a) Leukotriene B4 (LTB4), a pro-inflammatory mediator. b) Leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 (LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4), which act as airway constrictors. c) The 5-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (5-HETE) family and 5-oxo-eicosatetraenoic acid, which are mediators of pro-inflammatory and pro-allergic reactions. ALOX5 also contributes to the metabolism of arachidonic acid and other polyunsaturated fatty acids into specialized pro-resolving mediators, such as lipoxins and resolvins, which help to resolve inflammation and allergic reactions. In vitro studies suggest that COTL1 functions to stabilize ALOX5 by acting as a chaperone or scaffold. This stabilization prevents the inactivation of ALOX5 and enhances its metabolic activity.
